summary: Describes architectural considerations of using a Name Resolution Service in Information-Centric Networking, including how it changes the architecture and affects the ICN routing system. It is a product of the ICN Research Group and is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A directory that maps names of content to where it can be found.

questions: how does a name resolution service help icn routing
what is producer mobility in icn
subtitle: Mapping content names to their locations in a next-generation Internet.

tldr.problem: Information-Centric Networking uses content names to route data, but pure name-based routing has scaling challenges and cannot efficiently support moving producers or off-path caches.
tldr.mechanism: A Name Resolution Service (NRS) acts as a directory that maps content names to routable locations, allowing the routing system to handle queries dynamically instead of storing every possible name.
tldr.outcome: An NRS reduces routing table size and enables producer mobility and off-path caching, though it introduces latency and new security considerations that the system must address.

today: RFC 9236 is informational and represents the consensus of the Information-Centric Networking Research Group. ICN remains a research topic, and the NRS approach is an active area of investigation in several academic and research projects.

sections.title: What is Information-Centric Networking and the Name Resolution Service
sections.content:
Information-Centric Networking (ICN) is a redesign of how the Internet works. Instead of routing to machines by their addresses, ICN routes packets by the name of the data being requested. Two major ICN architectures are Named Data Networking (NDN) and Content-Centric Networking (CCNx). Both use content names directly for routing, much like asking for a book by title instead of asking for a book at a specific shelf.

However, pure name-based routing faces three key problems: (1) the routing table can grow too large if too many unique content names are published, similar to DNS becoming overwhelmed if it had to track every book in every library; (2) when a content producer moves to a new location, all downstream routers must be updated; and (3) finding copies of content stored off the main delivery path is complex.

A Name Resolution Service (NRS) addresses these challenges by acting as a directory. Instead of routing by name alone, an NRS translates a content name into routable information such as a location, a pointer to a cached copy, or an alias. This allows the routing system to work dynamically, asking the NRS only when needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of knowing where everything is, a router can ask a directory: 'Who has this content and where?' The directory answers quickly, and the router knows where to send the request.

sections.title: The Routing Challenges That NRS Solves
sections.content:
The routing challenge in ICN mirrors scalability issues in IP routing. When a router's forwarding table becomes too large, it cannot function efficiently. In ICN, if many different content names are published, the routing table grows uncontrolled, especially in the core of the network where many routes converge.

A second challenge is producer mobility. In ICN with hierarchical naming, if a content producer moves to a different network domain with a new name prefix, every router that might route to that content must learn the new location. This is harder than in ICN systems with flat naming. Several real ICN projects have adopted an NRS specifically to handle producer movement, translating old content names to new locations on the fly.

A third challenge is off-path caching. In-network caching is common in ICN, but caches that sit off the main path from producer to consumer cannot be discovered through simple name-based routing. The NRS can track the locations of off-path cached copies, allowing consumers to retrieve content from the nearest replica, reducing latency and network load.
sections.plainLanguage: Three problems: (1) routers run out of memory tracking every name, (2) when a producer moves, every router needs to know the new address, and (3) cached copies sitting on the side are hard to find. A directory solves all three.

sections.title: How an NRS Changes the ICN Architecture
sections.content:
Adding an NRS to ICN changes the architecture in three ways. First, the forwarding procedure changes. Instead of routing by name alone, a router now first checks its local routing table. If the name is not found, it asks the NRS for routing information and updates its table before forwarding the request. This adds a name-resolution step before each unknown content request.

Second, latency increases due to the NRS lookup, but this can be offset by the ability to find the nearest cached copy. The trade-off is that while NRS lookup adds delay, the direct path to a nearby cache may reduce overall delivery time compared to routing to a distant producer.

Third, the security surface expands. An NRS introduces new entities (NRS servers) that can be attacked. Attackers might send false NRS responses, leading routers to incorrect locations, or launch denial-of-service attacks against the NRS itself. The integrity and availability of the NRS must be protected to maintain ICN security.
sections.plainLanguage: Now routers must ask the directory sometimes (slower for first request), but they can find closer copies (faster overall). Bad actors can attack the directory, so it needs protection.

sections.title: Deploying and Operating an NRS System
sections.content:
An NRS is typically deployed as a distributed system of servers, similar to how DNS works globally. When a producer creates new content and assigns it a name, it registers that name with an NRS server, providing routing information such as a routable prefix or a pointer to its location. Routers that handle off-path caching must also register cached content so other routers know where copies exist.

When a router or consumer cannot find a content name in its local forwarding table, it sends a name-resolution request to an NRS server. The server returns mapping information, which the router uses to update its forwarding table or to construct a tunnel to the content location. This can happen reactively (when a content request arrives) or proactively (a router pre-populates its table).

Names must be registered with an authoritative NRS server managed by the content publisher. The NRS stores not just one location but can store multiple locations if content is cached or replicated in several places. Each mapping record can include a lifetime or validity period, after which the router must refresh the information. This allows the NRS to track dynamic content movement.
sections.plainLanguage: Producers register their content with the directory. When a router needs to know where content is, it asks. The directory can list several places the content exists, and the router picks one.

sections.title: Security and Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
Three security concerns emerge. First, namespace security requires that content names are securely mapped to their publishers and that the publishers are authenticated. If an attacker can register false names or hijack a publisher's identity, consumers will be misled.

Second, NRS system security is critical. NRS servers can be targets of distributed denial-of-service attacks. Attackers might send enormous numbers of name-resolution requests, overloading the service. Secure communication between routers and NRS servers must prevent eavesdropping and tampering. The history of name resolutions should be logged to detect and investigate attacks.

Third, protocol and message security requires that NRS messages for registration, resolution, and updates are protected by integrity checks, authentication, and encryption. Unauthorized routers must not be able to register false names or modify resolution records.

When implementing an NRS, designers choose whether to extend existing ICN protocols (like CCNx) with NRS messages or to build NRS as a separate service with its own protocol, such as a RESTful API. The choice affects complexity and flexibility.
sections.plainLanguage: The directory must prevent fake registrations, resist attacks, and protect its data from being spied on or changed.
